subject: Career
title: The Power of Silence
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on The Power of Silence.

hook.text: You name your number. They say nothing. The silence is unbearable. You start negotiating against yourself.

buildup.text: Silence creates social pressure. Humans are wired to fill empty space with concessions.

discovery.text: Skilled negotiators use silence deliberately. After stating their position, they wait.

twist.text: The person who speaks first after a number is named usually concedes something.

climax.text: Practice sitting in silence for ten seconds after making a request. It feels eternal but works.

punchline.text: Say your number. Then stop talking.

quiz.question: Why is silence powerful in salary negotiation?
options: It creates pressure — whoever speaks first often concedes

details.summary: Strategic silence after stating a request forces the other party to respond rather than allowing you to negotiate against yourself. Skilled negotiators embrace the discomfort of pauses because silence transfers psychological pressure across the table.
details.whyItMatters: Most inexperienced negotiators fill silence by lowering their own ask. Learning to wait after a proposal is one of the highest-return negotiation skills.
takeaways: Silence transfers pressure to the other party to respond
Filling a pause often means negotiating against yourself
Practicing silence in low-stakes settings builds the habit

faq.question: How long should a strategic silence typically last?
faq.answer: Five to ten seconds is usually sufficient to create productive discomfort. The silence feels longer to both parties than it actually is. Maintaining calm eye contact and a neutral expression makes the pause feel confident rather than awkward.

faq.question: What if the other side also stays silent after my request?
faq.answer: If both sides pause, the first to speak should ask an open-ended question like 'What are your thoughts on that figure?' This keeps the conversation moving without conceding ground or weakening the original ask.
